title: Prediction markets allow the powerful to buy truth
subtitle: Betting on the future
author: Yasaman Rohanifar
introduction: Many claim that prediction markets demonstrate the wisdom of crowds, and accurately tell us the future. This assumption has led them to become widespread in governments, newsrooms, and AI systems, treated as a valuable source of knowledge. But in new research, Yasaman Rohanifar, Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed, and Sharifa Sultana argue this is a catastrophic misreading. Behind prediction markets' democratic facade lies a process of prediction laundering—one in which anonymous whales, political insiders, and coordinated capital manufacture consensus while the platforms ensure the public never sees the machinery behind it.
body:
The rules of public knowledge are changing. For decades, when citizens, policymakers, and financial institutions needed to gauge the likelihood of a major world event, they turned to traditional pillars of authority such as intelligence briefings, journalist reports, statistical pollsters, and panels of academic experts. Today, that legacy informational infrastructure is being bypassed by raw financial mechanisms instead. The trading prices of decentralized prediction platforms like Polymarket have evolved from niche internet curiosities into the new global norm for establishing political and social facts.

The scale of this trend is massive, and it is accelerating. Leading global financial networks have officially integrated live prediction market feeds into their flagship terminal frameworks, treating speculative contract fluctuations with the same institutional seriousness as sovereign bond yields or corporate equity streams. At the same time, major media conglomerates are restructuring their reporting around these metrics, routinely citing market odds as definitive proof of public sentiment rather than relying on traditional polling data. Perhaps most significantly, prediction market data has migrated into the automated computational systems that govern daily digital life. Conversational artificial intelligence tools and large language model search engines now scrape these market percentages in real time, serving them directly to millions of everyday users as the objective truth regarding complex geopolitical conflicts and domestic policy decisions.

This institutional adoption is driven by the premise that financial markets possess a unique capacity to aggregate dispersed human knowledge efficiently. Proponents argue that because traders must put their money where their mouth is, backing their assertions with capital, the resulting price signal acts as a more honest distillation of global opinion. This view is not unfounded—the Iowa Electronic Markets consistently outperformed major polling aggregators in forecasting US presidential elections across multiple cycles. Controlled experiments have demonstrated that prediction markets can outperform both individual experts and conventional survey instruments when the conditions are right.

However, treating the speculative percentages produced by platforms like Polymarket as neutral information carries a risk. As public debate intensifies over the expansion of commercial predictive speculation into new international jurisdictions, critics have increasingly challenged their perceived neutrality. Prediction market platforms function less like democratic public squares and more like predatory, unregulated financial spaces that can actively incentivize the manipulation of public opinion and insider trading.

Behind the authoritative digital facade lies a complex social and financial machine. The apparently clean, unbiased numbers consumed by media networks and AI models are the output of a multi-stage pipeline we might think of as “prediction laundering”: a structural process by which highly strategic financial bets are systematically scrubbed of their context to present a mirage of objective truth to the external world.

So how does the laundry cycle work? There are four distinct stages of how a prediction is manufactured.

First comes the gatekeeping. Polymarket and platforms like it are marketed as open, egalitarian crowd-sourcing machines, where anyone can theoretically suggest a topic. In reality, ordinary participants do not possess the structural capability to directly create or list a contract. A centralized, internal markets team acts as a strict institutional gatekeeper, deciding exactly which versions of the events are permitted to enter the arena of trade. Proposals are vetted based on their ongoing news value, external trading demand, and how seamlessly they can be resolved on a blockchain ledger. The platform dictates which futures are deemed “bet-able.”

A single ultra-wealthy trader, or a “whale,” can dump millions of dollars into a specific position, single-handedly overriding public sentiment.

This creates an environment where geopolitical and social crises are prioritized by their capacity to attract liquid capital and trading volume. For instance, high-volume contracts tracking the daily micro-movements of high-profile Western political scandals or mainstream regulatory decisions dominate the front page because they tap into pre-existing media feeds where heavy capital is eager to flow.

Meanwhile, humanitarian emergencies or crises in under-reported regions are pushed to the margins, or even excluded entirely, because they lack the speculative traction required to generate platform fees. In rejecting complex or low-liquidity situations, this gatekeeping shapes the boundaries of public awareness. The only versions of reality allowed to achieve public authority are those that have been pre-sanitized for corporate speculation.

The second stage flattens diverse motivations and beliefs into one probabilistic lump. Once a contract goes live, people trade for wildly different reasons: data-driven analysis, emotional bias, financial hedging, or pure speculation. For instance, a participant might place a massive wager against their preferred political candidate purely as financial insurance to soften the blow of a loss. Although they are not expressing a genuine belief, the platform cannot express this difference. Its pricing mechanism dissolves the intent, the doubt, and the strategy behind every dollar, flattening everything into a singular percentage. The casual observer has no way of knowing what a number really means.

Third, the platform presents its fluctuating percentages as the democratic wisdom of crowds. But, because participants are pseudonymous, a single ultra-wealthy trader, or a “whale,” can dump millions of dollars into a specific position, single-handedly overriding public sentiment and forcing the price momentum upward. This disproportionately empowers individuals with privileged access to information, such as insiders, political operators, or tech elites who hold a distinct upper hand over the average observer. This means well-positioned actors can leverage private knowledge to execute massive, coordinated trades before the information becomes public.

This selective opacity creates an asymmetry of knowledge. Technical elites can use complex blockchain explorers to trace individual digital wallets and spot this manipulation in real time, but the general public, lacking the same tools and literacy, consumes the front-end price at face value. They are left completely unaware that the democratic “crowd” they think they are listening to could actually be a number of wealthy individuals or insiders moving the market momentum to protect their own financial positions.

The final stage occurs when a market expires and must settle into a historical fact. When real-world events are ambiguous, the resolution process relies on a stratified financial hierarchy where participants stake bonds to vote on outcomes. Our audit tracked traders flooding off-platform channels like Discord with tactical deception and biased information to protect their money. Behind that apparently decisive market verdict is a whole history of hidden friction that the public never gets to know about.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Guesses, errors and economics With Guy Standing, Linda Yueh, Gillian Tett, Richard Werner

Prediction laundering, therefore, introduces a serious accountability gap. By turning the human body politic into speculative puzzles on a chart, the interface performs a form of moral laundering, too. It allows individuals to profit from disaster while shifting the ethical burden onto the perceived neutrality of the market. The dangers of this only accelerate when these numbers leak out of the crypto ecosystem. When policy-makers or news networks treat a Polymarket percentage as an objective indicator of reality, they complete the laundry cycle. They grant institutional legitimacy to a signal forged in extreme capital asymmetry, allowing private wealth to masquerade as public intelligence.

Could these prediction markets be reformed to deliver on their promises? To do so, contrary to the standard Silicon Valley obsession with frictionless efficiency, there is a critical need to introduce what we call “friction-positive” design, with the aim of bringing to the surface the complex social and financial mechanics hidden beneath the numbers. The platform would need to integrate prominent whale alerts and capital concentration metrics directly onto the public front-end user interface. When an observer can see at a glance that a 75% probability is being manufactured by only two digital wallets, the illusion of a broad public consensus naturally dissipates.

Platforms could also implement multi-signal disclosure mechanisms that allow traders to explicitly tag the underlying intent behind their capital allocation. Clearly distinguishing an active conviction bet from a financial hedge helps prevent the public distortion that occurs when risk-management insurance is misread as a literal prediction.

Finally, platforms should retain a permanent link between a finalized page and its real-time history of dispute resolution logs, community arguments, and oracle votes, to ensure essential context is preserved. A settled fact is most reliable when it is never permitted to detach from its historical pedigree.

While these platforms operate as incredibly sophisticated computational systems, they do not function as neutral, passive mirrors of human belief. They act as active intervention tools that directly influence public perception. Moving toward designs that expose, rather than obscure, underlying financial asymmetries and social friction is an essential step toward preserving the clarity and health of public discourse.
